title: Farming begins
place: Jericho and the Fertile Crescent (southern Levant)
summary: In the Fertile Crescent, people began cultivating wild cereals such as barley around 9500 BCE and settled in permanent villages like Jericho, founded beside a spring between about 9500 and 9000 BCE. Over the following one to two thousand years emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, lentils, peas, chickpeas, bitter vetch and flax became fully domesticated crops, and the region's wild sheep, goats, cattle and pigs became farm animals.
why: Farming fed far more people from the same land than hunting and gathering, making possible permanent villages, food surpluses, growing populations and, in time, towns, specialists and states.
also: Farming was invented independently in several other places: rice and millet in China (rice domesticated between about 13,500 and 8,200 years ago), taro and yams at Kuk in New Guinea (perhaps from 8000 BCE), squash and maize in Mesoamerica (maize from about 7000 BCE), potatoes and manioc in South America, sorghum and pearl millet in Africa, and sunflowers and other seed plants in eastern North America (c. 2500 BCE).

title: Çatalhöyük, an early proto-city
summary: On the Konya plain of Anatolia, farmers built a tightly packed settlement of mudbrick houses with no streets: people walked across the rooftops and climbed down into their homes by ladder. Houses were plastered and decorated with wall paintings and bull horns, and the dead were buried beneath the floors. Older estimates put its population at 5,000 or more; recent excavations suggest perhaps 600–800 people in a typical year of its middle phase.
why: Çatalhöyük shows early farmers living together in large numbers for some 2,000 years without palaces, temples or obvious rulers, making it a key site for understanding the step from village life towards towns.

title: Copper smelting begins
place: Belovode, near Petrovac na Mlavi (eastern Serbia)
summary: At Belovode, a village of the Vinča culture in the Balkans, copper slag dated to about 5000 BCE is the oldest securely dated evidence of smelting copper from ore at high temperature. Within a few centuries metal was spreading across south-eastern Europe: the cemetery at Varna on the Black Sea coast (c. 4600–4300 BCE) held copper tools and some 3,000 gold objects, often called the oldest gold treasure in the world.
why: Smelting turned rock into tools, ornaments and portable wealth, opening the Copper Age, and rich graves like those at Varna show metal sharpening the divide between elites and everyone else.
also: Early copper-working is also documented in the Near East, and around the North American Great Lakes people of the Old Copper complex cold-hammered native copper from about 6500 BCE, though without smelting it.

sources.title: Radivojević, Archaeometallurgy of the Vinča culture: Belovode in eastern Serbia (Historical Metallurgy 47)

title: The wheel and the plough
summary: Wheeled vehicles appear almost at once across a wide area in the second half of the 4th millennium BCE: a pot from Bronocice in Poland (c. 3600–3400 BCE) is incised with a four-wheeled wagon, pictographs from Uruk show wagons around 3500–3350 BCE, and the oldest surviving wooden wheel, from the Ljubljana Marshes in Slovenia, dates to about 3340–3030 BCE. In the same era farmers in the Near East harnessed oxen to the ard, a simple scratch plough, part of a wider shift to using animals for pulling, milk and wool.
why: Animal power multiplied the land a farming family could work and the loads it could move, opening up new land and making heavy overland transport practical.
also: In Mesoamerica the wheel was invented independently but was used only on small wheeled toys, never for transport before the 16th century.

title: Writing is invented
summary: In the temple district of Uruk, scribes began pressing signs into clay tablets around 3300 BCE to keep accounts of grain, animals and labour, a system that grew out of older clay accounting tokens. This proto-cuneiform developed into cuneiform, used for Sumerian, Akkadian and many other languages for some 3,000 years. In Egypt, labels from tomb U-j at Abydos (c. 3400–3200 BCE) show the beginnings of hieroglyphs, usually counted as a separate invention.
why: Writing let people store information beyond human memory, run large states and economies, and record laws, letters and literature; it marks the line between prehistory and history.
also: Writing was invented independently at least twice more: in Shang China (oracle-bone inscriptions, c. 1250 BCE) and in Mesoamerica, where Maya inscriptions date from the 3rd century BCE and possible earlier Olmec writing is debated.

title: Uruk, the first great city
summary: In the Late Uruk period, Uruk grew to some 250 hectares and perhaps 25,000–50,000 people, with tens of thousands more in its surrounding territory, the largest urban area in the world at the time. Its walled Eanna temple district had monumental temples, administrators using cylinder seals and tablets, and mass-produced ration bowls, and Uruk-style outposts spread from western Iran to south-eastern Anatolia.
why: Uruk is the earliest clear example of a city-state, with social classes, full-time specialists, temples and bureaucrats, a pattern of urban life soon repeated across Mesopotamia.

title: Egypt is unified
summary: Kings from Upper (southern) Egypt took control of the Nile Delta, completing a unification begun by earlier rulers. The Narmer Palette, found at Nekhen, shows King Narmer, usually identified with the legendary Menes, wearing the crowns of both Upper and Lower Egypt. The First Dynasty ruled from Memphis, where the Nile valley meets the delta.
why: Unification created a single kingdom along the Nile under one king, with writing and a bureaucracy, and pharaonic rule endured, with interruptions, for about 3,000 years.

title: Bronze comes into wide use
place: Anatolia and Mesopotamia (Kestel tin mine, southern Türkiye)
summary: Metalworkers found that adding arsenic or, better, tin to copper made a harder alloy, bronze. Arsenical bronze came first (the Maykop culture of the North Caucasus used it by the mid-4th millennium BCE), and by about 3000 BCE the Bronze Age had begun across much of the Old World, from Mesopotamia and Egypt to the Indus. Because tin is rare, bronze depended on long-distance trade; Kestel in southern Türkiye was mined for tin from about 3250 BCE.
why: Bronze tools and weapons were tougher than copper ones, and the hunt for tin and copper tied distant regions together in the first long-distance metal trade networks.
also: A tin-bronze foil from Pločnik in Serbia may date to c. 4650 BCE, though its dating is disputed. In China bronze-working took hold later, with early centres in the north-west by c. 2500–2300 BCE and large-scale casting at Erlitou.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Tin sources and trade in ancient times

title: Caral, first cities of the Americas
summary: On Peru's dry north-central coast, the Caral–Supe (Norte Chico) civilisation built the earliest known monumental centres in the Americas, with large-scale construction from about 3200 BCE. Caral itself, inhabited from about 2600 to 2000 BCE, had six monumental complexes each built around a pyramid, sunken circular plazas and around 3,000 residents. Its people irrigated cotton for fishing nets and textiles, ate fish and shellfish as well as crops, and made no pottery.
why: Caral shows that cities and monumental architecture arose in the Americas entirely independently, and almost as early as in Egypt and Mesopotamia.

title: Indus Valley cities flourish
summary: In its mature phase the Indus civilisation built planned cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, each with perhaps 30,000–60,000 people, laid out on grids with baked-brick houses and covered street drains. Spread over more than 1,000 settlements from Afghanistan and Balochistan to Gujarat, it covered a larger area than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined, yet no clear palaces or temples have been found and its script is still undeciphered.
why: The Indus cities were among the world's first urban societies, with some of the earliest known city sanitation, and show that early urban life could flourish without obvious palaces or royal monuments.

title: The Great Pyramid rises
summary: For the Fourth Dynasty pharaoh Khufu, Egyptians built the Great Pyramid at Giza, originally about 146.6 m tall, over roughly 26 years. Excavated workers' camps point to organised, conscripted labour rather than slaves, perhaps 13,000 on average and up to about 40,000 at peak, and the papyrus diary of an official named Merer records limestone being shipped to the site in Khufu's 27th year.
why: It was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for more than 3,700 years and shows how far an early state could organise labour, food supply and engineering.

title: Sargon builds the first empire
summary: Sargon, who in later legend began as cupbearer to the king of Kish, defeated Lugal-zage-si of Uruk around 2300 BCE, took control of Sumer to the Persian Gulf, and campaigned from Elam in Iran to Mari and Syria. He ruled from Akkad, a city whose site has never been found, and at its height around 2250 BCE his dynasty's empire reached from the Mediterranean to Iran.
why: Often called the world's first empire (historians debate the label), Akkad set the pattern of one king ruling many conquered cities and peoples, with a professional army and Akkadian as a shared language of government.

title: Horses and war chariots
summary: Ancient DNA shows that the ancestors of nearly all modern domestic horses were domesticated around 2200 BCE in the Volga–Don region of the western Eurasian steppe. Soon after, people of the Sintashta culture east of the Urals, who built fortified settlements such as Arkaim, buried light chariots with spoked wheels, the oldest known, in graves dated to around 2000 BCE, often together with these horses.
why: Fast horses and chariots transformed warfare, travel and communication: within about 500 years chariots appeared in Greece, Egypt and Mesopotamia, and they reached Shang China around 1200 BCE.

title: Code of Hammurabi
summary: Late in his reign (c. 1792–1750 BCE), King Hammurabi of Babylon had about 282 laws carved on a 2.25 m basalt stele crowned by an image of the sun god Shamash. The laws cover trade, wages, family and property, set penalties that differed by social class, and include the principle of an eye for an eye. Centuries later the stele was carried off to Susa in Iran as plunder; it was found there in 1901 and is now in the Louvre.
why: It is the best-known early law collection, a ruler's public statement of fixed rules for justice, and it made the idea of written, displayed law famous across the ages.
also: It was not the first: the earlier Mesopotamian law collections of Ur-Nammu, Lipit-Ishtar and Eshnunna are known.

sources.title: Louvre: Law Code of Hammurabi, King of Babylon

title: The Vedas are composed
summary: In the north-west of the Indian subcontinent, poets composed the Rigveda, 1,028 hymns in Vedic Sanskrit, most likely between about 1500 and 1000 BCE, and it was gathered into a fixed collection around 1200–1000 BCE. Passed down orally with remarkable precision for many centuries before being written down, it was followed by the other Vedas and, from roughly the 7th–6th centuries BCE (dates are debated), by the philosophical Upanishads.
why: The Vedas are the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, and the Upanishads' ideas of brahman, atman and karma became central to Indian religion and philosophy.

title: Shang bronzes and oracle bones
summary: At Yin, the last capital of the Shang dynasty near modern Anyang, kings consulted their ancestors by cracking turtle shells and ox shoulder blades with heat and carving the questions and answers onto them. These oracle-bone inscriptions, beginning in the reign of Wu Ding around 1250 BCE, are the earliest substantial body of Chinese writing, with around 5,000 different characters. The same court cast magnificent bronze ritual vessels, like those in the tomb of Fu Hao, Wu Ding's consort and a war leader.
why: The oracle-bone script is the ancestor of the Chinese characters still in use today, making Chinese one of the world's longest continuously used writing systems.

title: Olmec civilisation flourishes
summary: In the tropical lowlands of Mexico's Gulf Coast, the Olmecs built San Lorenzo, the largest city in Mesoamerica from about 1200 to 900 BCE, before La Venta became their leading centre (c. 900–400 BCE). They carved colossal stone heads up to about 3 m tall and weighing many tonnes, probably portraits of rulers, and buried rich offerings of jade and serpentine.
why: Often called the mother culture of Mesoamerica (a debated label), the Olmecs pioneered monumental art and possibly ideas such as the ballgame and the Long Count calendar that shaped later civilisations like the Maya.

title: Late Bronze Age collapse
summary: Within a few decades around 1200 BCE, the interconnected palace kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean fell apart. The Hittite Empire broke up, the Mycenaean palaces of Greece were abandoned, and the port of Ugarit was destroyed around 1190–1185 BCE, its last letters warning of enemy ships; Egypt and Assyria survived but were weakened. Recent studies suggest fewer cities were destroyed than once believed.
why: The collapse ended an age of palace-run kingdoms and long-distance trade and cleared the way for the Iron Age world of new peoples, iron tools and the alphabet; its causes probably combined drought, earthquakes, migrations including the Sea Peoples, and fragile, over-centralised states.

title: Iron working spreads
summary: Iron had long been known in small amounts, from meteorites and occasional smelting, but around 1300–1200 BCE smiths in Anatolia and neighbouring regions mastered smelting iron ore, which needs far higher temperatures than bronze. In the 12th and 11th centuries BCE ironworking spread across the eastern Mediterranean, and smiths learned to harden iron into steel by heating it in charcoal and quenching it. The old idea that the Hittites guarded the secret of iron is no longer accepted.
why: Iron ore is far more common than tin, so once smelting was mastered, iron tools and weapons became cheap and widespread, transforming farming and warfare.
also: Iron was worked early, and probably independently, elsewhere: in India's Ganges plain from about 1800–1200 BCE, in sub-Saharan Africa (see Nok), and in China, which was making cast iron by the 5th century BCE.

title: The Phoenician alphabet
summary: Phoenician scribes in coastal cities such as Byblos used a script of just 22 letters, each standing for a consonant, developed from the earlier Proto-Sinaitic script, which was itself derived from Egyptian hieroglyphs. Its conventional starting date is c. 1050 BCE, and the inscription on the sarcophagus of King Ahiram of Byblos, usually dated to around 1000 BCE, is the earliest known example of the fully developed alphabet.
why: Carried by Phoenician traders around the Mediterranean, it became the ancestor of the Greek and Latin alphabets and, through Aramaic, of the Hebrew and Arabic scripts; a couple of dozen letters made reading and writing far easier to learn than systems with hundreds of signs.
also: At Ugarit, scribes had earlier used a 30-letter alphabet written in cuneiform wedges (c. 1400 BCE), whose letter order resembles the Phoenician.

title: Lapita voyagers reach Polynesia
summary: The Lapita people, Austronesian-speaking seafarers known for their pottery decorated with toothed stamps, had settled the Bismarck Archipelago off New Guinea by about 1600–1200 BCE. After 1200 BCE they sailed east into previously uninhabited islands, reaching Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji, and high-precision dating puts their founding settlement at Nukuleka in Tonga, the first landfall in Polynesia, at about 890 BCE.
why: Crossing hundreds of kilometres of open ocean in outrigger canoes, the Lapita began the human settlement of Remote Oceania, which their Polynesian descendants would later carry across the Pacific.

sources.title: Burley, Weisler & Zhao (2012), High Precision U/Th Dating of First Polynesian Settlement, PLoS ONE

title: First Olympic Games
summary: According to tradition, the first Olympic Games were held in 776 BCE at the sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia, with a single footrace, the stadion, won by Koroibos of Elis; archaeology suggests major games began nearer 700 BCE. Held every four years for free-born Greek men, the games were protected by a sacred truce for travellers and continued until the late 4th century CE or a little later.
why: The four-year Olympiad became a common Greek way of dating events, the games gave rival Greek city-states a shared festival and identity, and they inspired the modern Olympic Games.

title: Iron smelting in West Africa
summary: The Nok culture of central Nigeria, famous for its hollow, near life-sized terracotta sculptures, was smelting iron in bloomery furnaces by about 550 BCE and perhaps from 750 BCE or earlier. Excavations at Taruga uncovered iron slag, clay furnace pipes and wrought iron, helping to show that the Nok people lived in an Iron Age.
why: Early dates at Nok and other sites match or predate known ironworking at Carthage and Meroë, so many archaeologists now argue that iron smelting was invented independently south of the Sahara, though the evidence is still debated.
also: Even earlier smelting dates claimed for sites in Niger (Termit, c. 1500 BCE) and Nigeria (Lejja) remain disputed.

title: First coins in Lydia
summary: In Lydia and the neighbouring Greek cities of Ionia, the first coins, small lumps of electrum (a natural gold–silver alloy) stamped with a design, were struck in the late 7th century BCE; the electrum coin of Phanes from Ephesus dates to about 625–600 BCE. Around 550 BCE King Croesus issued the first coins of refined gold and silver, and workshops for separating electrum into pure gold and silver have been excavated at the Lydian capital, Sardis.
why: Coins of guaranteed weight and purity made trade, taxes and paying soldiers far simpler, and coinage soon spread through the Greek and Persian worlds.
also: In China, shovel-shaped bronze coins were cast at a mint in Henan between about 640 and 550 BCE, a separate tradition; India's punch-marked coins followed by the 4th century BCE, possibly earlier.

title: Cyrus founds the Persian Empire
summary: Cyrus II, king of Anshan in Persis, overthrew his Median overlord Astyages around 550 BCE and built his capital, Pasargadae, near the site of his victory. He went on to conquer Lydia (546 BCE) and Babylon (539 BCE), where the Cyrus Cylinder presents him as a restorer of temples and of displaced peoples; the Bible credits him with letting exiled Jews return to Jerusalem.
why: By his death in 530 BCE the Achaemenid Persian Empire stretched from Asia Minor to the Indus, the largest empire the world had yet seen, uniting many peoples, languages and religions under one king.

title: Democracy in Athens
summary: The reformer Cleisthenes reorganised the citizens of Athens into ten tribes based on where they lived rather than on family, created a Council of 500 chosen by lot, and strengthened the Assembly, where any adult male citizen could speak and vote. He called the system isonomia, equality before the law.
why: Athens became the best-known early democracy, where ordinary citizens debated and decided policy directly, though women, slaves and foreign residents were excluded, so voters were a minority of adults.

title: The Axial Age thinkers
place: Bodh Gaya (Bihar, India) and across Eurasia
summary: Within a few centuries, thinkers across Eurasia laid the foundations of lasting religions and philosophies: the Buddha (enlightened at Bodh Gaya; his dates are debated, c. 563–483 or c. 480–400 BCE) and Mahavira in India, Confucius (traditionally 551–479 BCE) and, according to tradition, Laozi in China, the Hebrew prophets in Israel, and Greek philosophers from Heraclitus and Parmenides to Plato. In 1949 the philosopher Karl Jaspers named this period, roughly the 8th to 3rd centuries BCE, the Axial Age.
why: Buddhism, Jainism, Confucianism, Daoism, the prophetic tradition of Judaism and Greek philosophy still shape the ethics and beliefs of billions of people; scholars debate whether this was one connected shift or a convenient label for separate developments.

title: The Persian Wars
summary: After Athens helped the Ionian Greeks revolt against Persia, King Darius sent an expedition that the Athenians and Plataeans defeated at Marathon in 490 BCE. In 480 BCE Xerxes invaded with a far larger force, won at Thermopylae and sacked an evacuated Athens, but lost the sea battle of Salamis; Greek victories at Plataea and Mycale in 479 BCE ended the invasion.
why: Greek independence survived, Athens rose as a naval power at the head of the Delian League, and its classical age followed; Herodotus' account of the wars earned him the title Father of History.

title: Alexander's conquests
summary: Alexander III of Macedon crossed into Asia in 334 BCE, beat the Persians at the Granicus, Issus (333) and Gaugamela (331), took Egypt, where he founded Alexandria, and overthrew the Achaemenid Empire. He pushed on to the Indus, defeating King Porus at the Hydaspes in 326 BCE, until his army refused to go further; he died at Babylon in 323 BCE, aged 32.
why: His conquests and the kingdoms of his successors spread Greek language and culture from Egypt to north-western India, opening the Hellenistic age in which Greek became a shared language across the region and cultures mixed, from Greco-Buddhist art to Alexandrian science.

title: Euclid and the Library of Alexandria
summary: In Alexandria, Ptolemy I founded the Mouseion, a research institute whose great library, probably established under Ptolemy II (r. 285–246 BCE), gathered somewhere between tens and hundreds of thousands of scrolls. Working in the city around 300 BCE, Euclid wrote the Elements, 13 books that build geometry and number theory step by step from definitions and postulates; later scholars there included Eratosthenes, who calculated the Earth's circumference.
why: The Elements was the core of mathematics teaching for some 2,000 years and has appeared in more than 1,000 printed editions, while the library became a lasting symbol of the ambition to collect all knowledge in one place.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Euclid

title: Ashoka turns from war
summary: In about the eighth year of his reign, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka conquered Kalinga on India's east coast; his own Rock Edict 13 records 100,000 killed and 150,000 carried off, and expresses deep remorse. He turned to dhamma, a moral code of non-violence and right conduct not tied to a single religion, proclaimed it in edicts carved on rocks and pillars across his empire, and became a lay follower and patron of Buddhism.
why: Ashoka is remembered as a ruler who renounced conquest by war, and the missionaries he is credited with sending, including his son Mahinda to Sri Lanka, helped Buddhism spread beyond India.

title: Qin unifies China
summary: After conquering the last of the rival Warring States, King Ying Zheng of Qin proclaimed himself Shi Huangdi, the First Emperor, in 221 BCE. He replaced hereditary lords with appointed officials in 36 commanderies and standardised the script, coins, weights, measures and even cart axle widths, while linking northern walls, building roads and ordering the burning of books from rival schools of thought.
why: Although the Qin dynasty fell in 206 BCE, after only 15 years, it created the centralised imperial system and common written script that held China together under emperors until 1911.

title: The Han dynasty begins
summary: Liu Bang, born into a peasant family, rose from minor Qin official to rebel leader, defeated his rival Xiang Yu at Gaixia and became emperor in 202 BCE, remembered as Emperor Gaozu of Han. Keeping much of the Qin's centralised system but easing its harsh laws and taxes, the Han ruled from Chang'an and, after a brief break (9–23 CE), from Luoyang until 220 CE.
why: Under the Han, Confucianism became the state ideology and a census of 2 CE counted some 57.7 million people; the dynasty became so central to Chinese identity that China's majority still call themselves the Han people and their writing Han characters.

title: Paper is invented in China
summary: The oldest surviving fragment of paper, apparently part of a map, was found at Fangmatan in Gansu and dates to about 179–141 BCE. Early paper made from plant fibres was used mostly for wrapping and padding, for example around bronze mirrors, and only later for writing. In 105 CE the court official Cai Lun refined papermaking using bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets, which is why he was long credited with inventing it.
why: Cheap, light paper gradually replaced bamboo, silk and parchment, reaching the Islamic world and then Europe by the 11th century, and made books and records far more widely available.

title: Rome destroys Carthage and Corinth
summary: In early 146 BCE, after a three-year siege in the Third Punic War, Roman troops under Scipio Aemilianus stormed Carthage, destroyed the city and sold some 50,000 survivors into slavery; its lands became the Roman province of Africa. In the same year Lucius Mummius defeated the Achaean League and sacked Corinth, bringing mainland Greece under direct Roman control.
why: With its great rival gone and Greece subdued, Rome became the unchallenged power of the Mediterranean, and the flood of Greek art and learning into Rome reshaped Roman culture.

title: The Silk Road opens
summary: Around 138 BCE Emperor Wu of Han sent the envoy Zhang Qian west to seek allies against the Xiongnu. After years as a Xiongnu captive he reached Dayuan (Ferghana), the Yuezhi and Bactria, and returned to Chang'an in 125 BCE with reports of rich states to the west. Han embassies, campaigns and trade followed, and by around 114 BCE a network of routes linked China with Central Asia and, in time, the Roman world.
why: For some 1,500 years the Silk Road carried silk, horses, paper and ideas across more than 6,400 km of Eurasia, linking civilisations that had known little of one another.

title: From Caesar to Augustus
summary: On 15 March 44 BCE, about 60 senators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed Julius Caesar, recently named dictator for life, in the Curia of Pompey in Rome. His heir Octavian joined Mark Antony and Lepidus in the Second Triumvirate, then defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE; in 27 BCE the Senate gave him the name Augustus.
why: Augustus became Rome's first emperor, ending the Republic and founding the Principate, a system of one-man rule behind republican forms that opened a long era of relative peace known as the Pax Romana.

title: Birth of Jesus
summary: Jesus of Nazareth was probably born between about 6 and 4 BCE, since the Gospels place his birth in the reign of King Herod, whose death is usually dated to 4 BCE. The Gospels of Matthew and Luke set his birth in Bethlehem, though many historians think he was more likely born in Nazareth in Galilee, where he grew up.
why: Christianity, which grew from his life and teachings, became one of the world's largest religions, and the Anno Domini year count devised by Dionysius Exiguus in 525 CE, which placed his birth a few years too late, underlies today's common calendar era.
